thm:weight-decomposition-exists: Theorem Existence of the weight decomposition. For any quantum observable universe, the complementary projectors \pi_H and \pi_V exist on \Omega^k(A) and satisfy \pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}, alongside the idempotency conditions \pi_H^2 = \pi_H and \pi_V^2 = \pi_V.
prf:weight-decomposition-exists: Proof Proof of existence of the weight decomposition. The projections are constructed from the torus averaging operator: for each weight \lambda of the T-action, the \lambda-isotypic projector e_\lambda is idempotent, and \pi_H = e_0, \pi_V = \mathrm{id} - e_0.
ex:weight-decomposition-su2:
Example Constructive weight decomposition for \mathrm{SU}(2). For \mathrm{SU}(2), the weight decomposition is constructed explicitly via torus averaging. The maximal torus T = \mathrm{U}(1) acts on the coordinate ring A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) by left translation. On the matrix generators \alpha, \beta, \bar\alpha, \bar\beta, the action is diagonal, rescaling each generator by a phase.

For any integer weight m \in \mathbb{Z}, the isotypic projector is the Fourier integral:

  e_m(f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
    e^{-im\theta_q}\,(t_{\theta_q} \cdot f)\,d\theta_q.

The horizontal projector is \pi_H = e_0, while the vertical projector is \pi_V = \sum_{m \neq 0} e_m. The decomposition extends to the differential forms \Omega^k(A) via the Leibniz rule. Complementarity \pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id} follows from Fourier completeness, and idempotency from the orthogonality of characters.
rem:reeb-physical: Remark Physical interpretation of the weight decomposition. The geometric decomposition \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V enforces the spin-statistics connection at the categorical level. Purely horizontal forms carry integer spin and are bosons, while forms with non-trivial vertical components carry half-integer spin and are fermions.
sec:vectors-hadrons-intro: Having established the weight decomposition of forms, this section develops the trace and basis machinery for intertwiner spaces of tensor powers of the fundamental representation. It introduces the adjoint trace on endomorphisms, derived from the Frobenius pairing and the fibre-adjoint involution. This trace inherits cyclicity from the Frobenius relation and non-degeneracy from the positive-definiteness of the dagger. Next comes the Pawlowski--Leitner canonical basis on \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}). Indexed by standard Young tableaux with at most two rows, this basis emerges from contractions with the volume form along the unital Gröbner--Shirshov route, its dimension governed by the hook-length formula. Finally, the adjoint trace equips the PawLei basis with an orthogonal inner product. This pairing coincides with the Frobenius form restricted to \mathrm{End}(V_j), ensuring that fibre integration commutes with the intertwiner expansion of hadron states.
rem:adjoint-trace:
Remark Adjoint trace and the categorical inner product. The Frobenius pairing and the fibre-adjoint involution together equip every hom-space \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y) with a canonical sesquilinear form. The adjoint trace on endomorphisms of V is defined by

  \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f)
  = 
  \int_A \!\circ \mu \circ (f \otimes \mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}})
    \circ \mathrm{coev}_V
   \in 
  \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) \cong R,

where \mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V \otimes V^{\vee} is the coevaluation map and \mu is the Frobenius multiplication.

This trace is cyclic, \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f \circ g) = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(g \circ f), inherited directly from the Frobenius relation. It is also non-degenerate, as the induced pairing \langle f, g \rangle_{\mathrm{Ad}} = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f^{\dagger} \circ g) inherits non-degeneracy from the Frobenius integral and positivity from the dagger structure. In the archimedean limit G = \mathrm{SU}(2), the adjoint trace recovers the Killing form on \mathfrak{su}(2): \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{ad}(f)) = -2\mathrm{tr}_{\mathbb{C}^2}(f).
prop:pawlowski-leitner-basis:
Proposition Pawlowski--Leitner basis for \mathrm{Hom}(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}). Let V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2 be the fundamental representation of G = \mathrm{SU}(2). For each simple object V_j and tensor power V_{1/2}^{\otimes n} with n \geq 2j, the intertwiner space \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr) admits a canonical PawLei basis. This basis is indexed by standard Young tableaux of shape \lambda \vdash n having at most two rows and satisfying \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 2j.

\begin{equation}\label{eq:pawlei-basis-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\epsilon^{\vee}"]
  & \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \ar[r, hook]
  & V_{1/2}^{\otimes n} \ar[r, "\pi_j"]
  & V_j
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The volume form \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \to \mathbf{1} and its dual \epsilon^{\vee} act as contraction operators. Each PawLei basis element is formed by applying a tableau-specified sequence of contractions to the highest-weight vector e_+^{\otimes (j+m)} \otimes e_-^{\otimes (j-m)}, followed by row symmetrization.

The dimension of the intertwiner space follows the hook-length formula:

  \dim\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr)
  = 
  \frac{(2j+1) n!}{(\tfrac{n}{2}+j+1)!(\tfrac{n}{2}-j)!}

for n \equiv 2j \pmod{2}, and vanishes otherwise.
rem:pawlowski-leitner-basis-construction: Remark PBW derivation of the Pawlowski--Leitner basis. The construction relies on the PBW theorem over commutative rings: the unital Gröbner--Shirshov basis for U(\mathfrak{su}(2)) provides a monomial basis for the enveloping algebra, from which the intertwiner basis is derived by contraction with the volume form (the diagram of the Pawlowski--Leitner basis).
prop:pawlowski-leitner-inner-product:
Proposition Inner product on intertwiner spaces. The adjoint trace induces an inner product on the intertwiner spaces. For \phi, \psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}), define:

  \langle \phi, \psi \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}}
  = 
  \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}\!\bigl(\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi\bigr)
  = 
  \int_A \!\circ \mu \circ (\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \mathrm{coev}_{V_j}.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pawlei-inner-product-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev}_{V_j}"]
  & V_j \otimes V_j^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
  & A \otimes V_j^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\int_A \circ \mu"]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The PawLei basis \{T_{\lambda}\} is strictly orthogonal under this pairing: \langle T_{\lambda}, T_{\mu} \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}} = \delta_{\lambda\mu} \|T_{\lambda}\|^2, where the squared norm is a positive rational computable directly from the hook lengths of \lambda.

This orthogonality guarantees two physical structures. First, any categorical hadron state of valence n admits a unique, orthogonal expansion into partial-wave amplitudes. Second, the inner product coincides with the restriction of the Frobenius pairing to \mathrm{End}(V_j) \subset A. This compatibility ensures that integration over the gauge fibre commutes with the decomposition of physical states.
sec:differential-structures-intro: This section develops the first-order differential structure on the Frobenius--Hopf object A. This machinery includes the categorical Reeb derivation, the projective-line object, the affine chart it carries, and the fibre-adjoint involution. Each of these structures is forced by the QOU axioms. It constructs the categorical Reeb derivation (\xi, \varTheta_A) from the weight decomposition and realize it physically within the left-covariant calculus. The function-algebra quotient then forms the projective line object, which carries an intrinsic contact affine chart. Finally, the fibre-adjoint involution embeds the projective line as a coadjoint orbit, establishing the observability axiom directly from the Frobenius pairing.
def:categorical-reeb:
Definition Categorical Reeb derivation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with maximal torus T and weight decomposition \pi_H, \pi_V. The categorical Reeb derivation is the endomorphism \xi \colon A \to A generating the T-action. It acts as the infinitesimal generator of T \subset G via the adjoint coaction. It satisfies three conditions. First, it generates vertical forms: \pi_V \circ d = \iota_\xi d\varTheta_A, where \varTheta_A \in \Omega^1(A) is the canonical 1-form dual to \xi. Second, it is normalized: \varTheta_A(\xi) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}. Third, horizontal forms are precisely the kernel of contraction: \Omega^k_H(A) = \ker(\iota_\xi).

\begin{equation}\label{eq:reeb-decomposition-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\pi_H"] \ar[d, "\pi_V"']
  & \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[d, hook] \\
  \varTheta_A \wedge \Omega^{k-1}_H(A) \ar[r, hook]
  & \Omega^k(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
thm:categorical-reeb-exists:
Theorem Existence of the categorical Reeb derivation. For any quantum observable universe, there exists a unique categorical Reeb derivation (\xi, \varTheta_A) on A satisfying the vertical-generator constraint \pi_V \circ d = \iota_\xi d\varTheta_A and the normalization constraint \varTheta_A(\xi) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}.

\begin{equation}\label{eq:reeb-exists-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  A \ar[r, "\xi"] \ar[d, "d"']
  & A \ar[d, "\varTheta_A"] \\
  \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\iota_\xi"']
  & A
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
prf:categorical-reeb-exists: Proof Proof of existence of the categorical Reeb derivation. The derivation \xi is the infinitesimal generator of the one-parameter subgroup T \cong \mathrm{U}(1) \subset G, and \varTheta_A is its Maurer--Cartan dual, uniquely determined by the normalisation condition.
prop:categorical-reeb-unique: Proposition Uniqueness of the categorical Reeb derivation. The vertical-generator and normalization axioms together fix the derivation along the vertical distribution corresponding to the free T-action. The dual form is then uniquely determined by extending to the horizontal distribution via the Maurer--Cartan condition. Therefore, the categorical Reeb derivation is unique.
prf:categorical-reeb-unique: Proof Proof of uniqueness of the categorical Reeb derivation. By the vertical-generator axiom, \xi_i = \iota_{\xi_i} d\varTheta_A^{(i)} \circ (\pi_V \circ d)^{-1} on the vertical summand. Because T acts freely on A_V = \pi_V(A), the infinitesimal generator \xi_i is the unique lift of the T-action on A_V to an endomorphism of A — unique up to the Lie-algebra action of T, which is one-dimensional for T \cong U(1). The normalisation axiom \varTheta_A^{(i)}(\xi_i) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}} fixes the remaining scalar, so \xi_1 = \xi_2. Given equal \xi, the dual form \varTheta_A^{(i)} is determined by the Maurer--Cartan condition and horizontality on \pi_H(A), forcing \varTheta_A^{(1)} = \varTheta_A^{(2)}.
ex:reeb-su2: Example Reeb derivation for \mathrm{SU}(2). For G = \mathrm{SU}(2), the maximal torus T = \mathrm{U}(1) has the generator \xi = \frac{1}{2}\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix} \in \mathfrak{su}(2). On A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), \xi acts as the left-invariant vector field. The canonical 1-form is \varTheta_A = \omega_3, satisfying \omega_3(\xi) = 1. The horizontal forms are those with no \omega_3 component. In the archimedean realization on a CR manifold (M, \varTheta), \xi is the Reeb vector field with \iota_\xi d\varTheta = 0.
def:projective-line-object: Definition Projective line object. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe. The projective line object is the quotient \mathbb{P}(V) = G / T, realized in the category via its function algebra A^{\mathrm{co}T}, the T-coinvariant subalgebra of A.
rem:projective-line-object-remark: Remark The projective line object under the fibre functor. Under the canonical fibre functor, the projective line object manifests as the scheme-theoretic projective line \mathbb{P}^1(R).
ex:projective-line-su2: Example Projective line for \mathrm{SU}(2). For G = \mathrm{SU}(2), the quotient is \mathbb{P}(V) = \mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathrm{U}(1) \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}). A point in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) represents a line in V = \mathbb{C}^2. The corresponding function algebra is the polynomial ring \mathbb{C}[z] in the affine coordinate z = v_1 / v_2.
def:contact-affine-chart:
Definition Contact affine chart on \mathbb{P}(V). Let \mathbb{P}(V) be the projective line object. Using the Reeb decomposition, every form splits as \alpha = \alpha_H + \varTheta \wedge \iota_\xi \alpha. The contact affine chart U_\xi \subset \mathbb{P}(V) is the open dense subset where the Reeb component is non-vanishing:

  U_\xi =  \bigl\{ [\alpha] \in \mathbb{P}(V)
   \big|  \iota_\xi\alpha \neq 0 \bigr\}.

On U_\xi, the affine coordinate Z is defined as the ratio of the horizontal component to the vertical Reeb component:

  Z([\alpha]) =  \frac{\alpha_H}{\iota_\xi\alpha}.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contact-affine-chart-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  U_\xi \ar[r, hook] \ar[d, "Z"']
  & \mathbb{P}(V) \ar[d, "\cong"] \\
  H = \ker\varTheta \ar[r, hook]
  & \Omega^1_H(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The coordinate Z takes values in the horizontal distribution H.
rem:contact-affine-chart-remark: Remark The contact affine chart as an intrinsic stereographic projection. The contact form and the Reeb vector field supply the stereographic projection of \mathbb{P}(V) intrinsically, without external coordinates.
sec:differential-structures-fiber-adjoin: This section introduces the fibre-adjoint involution, closing the differential-structure machinery. This involution provides the projector onto coadjoint orbits and governs the aether's radial coordinate. It first establishes the fibre-functor atlas and define the involution. It then extracts the radial coordinate, confirm its well-definedness under the Reeb flow, and specialize the involution to \mathrm{SU}(2) in preparation for constructing the connection.
prop:fibre-functor-atlas: Proposition Fibre functors as an affine atlas with G-torsor transitions. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with gauge group G. For any two fibre functors \tau', \tau'' \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}, the space of monoidal natural isomorphisms \tau' \Rightarrow \tau'' forms a G-torsor, and functorial composition enforces the cocycle condition. Hence the category of all fibre functors of (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) forms a G-gerbe.
prf:fibre-functor-atlas:
Proof Proof of fibre functor atlas. (1) A fibre functor \tau' assigns to each object X in \mathbf{C} an R-module \tau'(X) and to each morphism f a linear map \tau'(f), preserving the tensor product. This is a concrete coordinate system for the abstract category — an affine chart.

(2) By the Tannaka–Krein theorem (\mathrm{SU}(2) emergence), any monoidal natural isomorphism \eta \colon \tau' \xrightarrow{\sim} \tau'' is determined by an element g \in G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) acting on the fibre. The set of all such isomorphisms is a principal homogeneous space for G — a G-torsor. For q^2 \neq 1 the group of points of \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) is the maximal torus T (Lean: QOU.AlgebraicSubstrate.OqSU2.charEquivUnits), so the transition functions take values in T and the atlas is a T-torsor, matching the \mathrm{U}(1) chart swap. The full G acts only at the symmetric point q = 1.

(3) If \eta_{01} \colon \tau' \to \tau'' and \eta_{12} \colon \tau'' \to \tau''' are monoidal natural isomorphisms, their composition \eta_{12} \circ \eta_{01} is the unique monoidal natural isomorphism \tau' \to \tau''' corresponding to the group product g_{12} \cdot g_{01}. The cocycle identity g_{02} = g_{12} \cdot g_{01} is the associativity of composition in the functor category.

(4) Connectedness: any two fibre functors are isomorphic (Tannaka–Krein). Simple transitivity: the isomorphism is unique up to G. \square
rem:fibre-functor-atlas-affine-charts: Remark Fibre-functor gerbe as the affine atlas. Every fibre functor \tau' \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod} serves as an affine chart, realizing the abstract categorical data over R; the canonical functor \tau yields the contact affine chart on \mathbb{P}(V). Under this reading each monoidal natural isomorphism acts as a transition function changing affine coordinates, so the G-gerbe of fibre functors is precisely the affine atlas of the quantum universe.
prop:fiber-adjoint-involution:
Proposition Fiber--adjoint-fiber involution. The Frobenius form \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} induces an isomorphism A \xrightarrow{ \sim } A^{\vee}. Under this self-duality, the projective line object \mathbb{P}(V) embeds into the adjoint object \mathrm{Ad}(A) as the coadjoint orbit of a highest-weight vector. This assignment \sigma \colon \mathbb{P}(V) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Ad}(A) is an involution, entirely determining \mathbb{P}(V) from \mathrm{Ad}(A) and vice versa. The non-degeneracy of the Frobenius pairing then forces the observability condition \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.

\begin{equation}\label{eq:fiber-adjoint-involution-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \mathbb{P}(V)
    \ar[r, hook, "\sigma"]
    \ar[d, "\cong"']
  & \mathrm{Ad}(A)
    \ar[d, "\cong", "\int_A"'] \\
  G/T
    \ar[r, hook, "\text{coadjoint orbit}"]
  & A^{\vee}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
lem:fai-projector-coadjoint-orbit: Lemma Rank-1 projectors embed \mathbb{P}(V) as a coadjoint orbit in \mathrm{Ad}(A). Let V \in \mathbf{C} be the standard representation, and let \rho \colon V \to V be a rank-1 projector. The traceless component \sigma(\rho) = \rho - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{id}_V \in \mathrm{Ad}(A) satisfies the involution (2\sigma(\rho))^2 = \mathrm{id}_V. This map \sigma identifies \mathbb{P}(V) \cong G/T with a closed coadjoint orbit in \mathrm{Ad}(A).
prf:fai-projector-coadjoint-orbit:
Proof Proof of the projector / coadjoint-orbit identification. (1) Embedding via rank-1 projectors. Let \rho \colon V \to V be a rank-1 projector in \mathbf{C}: an endomorphism satisfying \rho^2 = \rho and \mathrm{tr}(\rho) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}} (categorical trace via evaluation and coevaluation). Since V has categorical dimension 2, define the traceless component

  \sigma(\rho) = \rho - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{id}_V
   \in  \mathrm{Ad}(A).

This is well-defined because \mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\rho)) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 0. The set of such projectors is precisely \mathbb{P}(V) = G/T, the quotient by the maximal torus.

(2) The involution. Under the positive-definite involutive structure \dagger (involutive structure), every rank-1 projector satisfies \rho^{\dagger} = \rho (self-adjointness). Computing the square of the traceless component:

  \sigma(\rho)^2
  = \bigl(\rho - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{id}_V\bigr)^2
  = \rho^2 - \rho + \tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{id}_V
  = \tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{id}_V.

Thus 2\sigma(\rho) is an involution in \mathrm{End}(V): it squares to the identity. Geometrically, \sigma identifies \mathbb{P}(V) with a coadjoint orbit in \mathrm{Ad}(A). The orbit is closed by rigidity of \mathbf{C} and determines a sub-object of \mathrm{Ad}(A) isomorphic to \mathbb{P}(V). Conversely, given this sub-object, the stabiliser of any point is T, so \mathbb{P}(V) \cong G/T as G-spaces. \square
prf:fiber-adjoint-involution:
Proof Proof of Fiber--adjoint-fiber involution. The Frobenius isomorphism A \cong A^{\vee} sends a \mapsto \int_A \circ \mu(a \otimes -), which is non-degenerate by the Frobenius--Hopf axiom.

By (rank-1 projectors as a coadjoint orbit), the traceless components of rank-1 projectors give an involution 2\sigma(\rho) in \mathrm{End}(V) and identify \mathbb{P}(V) \cong G/T with a closed coadjoint orbit in \mathrm{Ad}(A).

(3) Observability. Suppose there exists a non-zero morphism f \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathrm{Ad}(A). Such a morphism would represent a G-invariant element in the adjoint representation. By the \mathrm{SU}(2) emergence theorem (\mathrm{SU}(2) emergence), the reconstructed gauge group is G \cong \mathrm{SU}(2), and \mathrm{Ad}(A) carries the irreducible adjoint representation \mathfrak{su}(2) (dimension 3). By Schur's lemma, the only intertwining morphism from the trivial representation \mathbf{1} to an irreducible non-trivial representation is the zero morphism. Therefore f = 0, contradicting the assumption.

Hence \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0. The non-degeneracy of \int_A excludes any hidden global symmetry: there is no non-trivial invariant section of the adjoint bundle. \square
ex:fiber-adjoint-su2:
Example Fiber--adjoint-fiber involution for \mathrm{SU}(2). For G = \mathrm{SU}(2) and V = \mathbb{C}^2, the projective line is \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}), and the adjoint object is \mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbb{R}^3. The embedding \sigma maps a line \ell = \mathrm{span}(v) to the traceless projector:

  \sigma([\ell]) =
  \frac{v v^{\dagger}}{\lVert v \rVert^2}
  - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{id}_V
  \in \mathfrak{su}(2).

This identifies \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) with the unit 2-sphere S^2 \subset \mathfrak{su}(2), the coadjoint orbit of \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{diag}(i, -i). Observability immediately follows: any G-fixed point in \mathfrak{su}(2) would be a scalar matrix, but the only traceless scalar is zero, ensuring \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.
ex:connection-su2: Example Connection and curvature on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). On A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) with its left-invariant calculus \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}, a connection is a covariant derivative abla f = df + \mathcal{A} \cdot f, where \mathcal{A} \in \Omega^1(A) is the connection 1-form. It satisfies the Leibniz rule abla(fg) = ( abla f)g + f(dg). The curvature F_ abla = d\mathcal{A} + \mathcal{A} \wedge \mathcal{A} \in \Omega^2(A) is strictly A-linear.
sec:substrate-parameter-preamble: This section promotes the aether parameter q from an algebraic device to a structural ingredient of the categorical deformation. It extracts q from the categorical braiding, identifying it as the eigenvalue governing the symmetric tensor channel. This links the microscopic categorical data directly to the macroscopic fluid parameter. It then establishes the \mathbb{G}_m-family of differentials and the categorical gauge group deformation from \mathrm{SU}(2) to \mathrm{SU}_q(2).
prop:braiding-eigenvalue-extraction:
Proposition Extraction of q from the braiding eigenvalues. Let V be the fundamental object with braiding c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V. The tensor square decomposes intrinsically into symmetric and antisymmetric eigenspaces: V \otimes V = S^2 V \oplus \Lambda^2 V. Because \Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbf{1}, c_{V,V} acts on it by a scalar \lambda_-. It acts on S^2 V by a scalar \lambda_+. The aether parameter is defined as:

  q  :=  \lambda_+,
  \qquad
  \lambda_- =  -q^{-1}.

The product \lambda_+ \lambda_- = -1 reflects the determinant constraint. These eigenvalues encode the Hecke relation (T - q)(T + q^{-1}) = 0 for T = \tau(c_{V,V}). When c_{V,V}^2 = \mathrm{id}, this gives q = 1. The macroscopic interpolation d_q = q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1}) \pi_V \circ d is thus governed exactly by the microscopic braiding.
rem:braiding-eigenvalue-extraction-novel:
Remark Mathematical novelty: q is extracted, not posited. The deformation parameter q enters the framework categorically rather than by hand. It is the eigenvalue of the braiding c_{V,V} on the symmetric summand of V \otimes V, named by the Hecke relation; the Tannaka--Krein reconstruction (the reconstruction proposition below) then recovers \mathrm{SU}_q(2) as \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau) with that same q. The parameter is read off structure the category already carries.

What this does not settle is the value. The braiding is assumed data — a braided monoidal category comes equipped with a braiding, and different braidings give different eigenvalues. Reading q off the braiding therefore fixes the parameter's role, not its magnitude. The aether value q_0 \approx 1.10998 is not obtained this way. It is the CAL-2 calibration, pinned by matching m_\mu/m_e = \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)/\hbar_q^2 against the measured lepton ratio (see the epistemic status of the calibrations in the Physical Observations chapter); in the words of that block, q_0 is defined to enforce the match.

The two statements live at different levels and neither implies the other. At the fibre level q is a formal parameter whose categorical meaning is the braiding eigenvalue. At the archimedean level q_0 is a number fixed by one of the three external calibration inputs (the three-calibration discipline of the Physical Observations chapter). A derivation of q_0 from the aether is not claimed here and is not part of the framework.

Using the Hecke relation and the determinant constraint to relate braiding eigenvalues is standard (Kassel). What the extraction buys is an identification: the parameter governing the macroscopic fluid PDE is the same object as the microscopic braiding eigenvalue, so the two descriptions share one parameter instead of two. That is a structural statement about which quantity appears where, and it is silent on what that quantity's value is.
prop:spectral-chart-correspondence: Proposition Spectral--chart correspondence: Hecke eigenspaces realise the chart-glue of \mathbb{P}_q(V). The Hecke spectral decomposition of V \otimes V directly specifies the chart-transition data on the projective line \mathbb{P}(V). On the two contact affine charts, the transition coordinate \kappa in z\,w = \kappa equals \lambda_+^{-1} = -\lambda_- = q^{-1}. The single scalar identity dictating the antisymmetric eigenvalue simultaneously fixes the geometric gluing of the quantum projective line.
prop:tannaka-krein-reconstruction: Proposition Tannaka--Krein reconstruction of the quantum gauge group. By Tannaka--Krein duality, the coend H = \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau) = \int^{X \in \mathbf{C}} \tau(X)^{\vee} \otimes_R \tau(X) carries a canonical Hopf algebra structure. This provides the monoidal equivalence \mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(H). For generic braiding, H reconstructs the compact quantum group algebra \mathcal{O}_q(G). The deformation parameter q is determined by the braiding.
def:aether-parameter:
Definition Aether parameter. The non-commutative de Rham complex carries two canonical endomorphisms: the full differential d and the vertical differential \pi_V \circ d. These span a one-parameter family of first-order operators:

  d_q =  q^{-1}d +  (1 - q^{-1})\pi_V \circ d.

The aether parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) is the unique value for which d_q acts as q^{-1}d on horizontal forms and as d on vertical forms.
rem:aether-parameter-limits-and-lusztig:
Remark Limits of the aether parameter and the Lusztig integral form. The family d_q of the definition, with its two limits:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:substrate-family-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "d"] \ar[d, "\pi_V \circ d"'] \ar[dr, "d_q"]
  & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \\
  \Omega^{k+1}(A)
  & {} \ar[u, phantom, "q{=}1"' near start]
    \ar[l, phantom, "q{\to}\infty" near start]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

At q = 1, d_q recovers d. As q \to \infty, d_q projects fully onto the Reeb direction. When realized physically over a base space M, q becomes a local aether field q \colon M \to k^{\times}. Algebraically, this corresponds to the Lusztig integral form \mathcal{U}^{\mathbb{Z}}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)), which undergoes a base change via q \mapsto q_0.
rem:q-generic-ground-ring:
Remark The q-generic ground ring. With the aether parameter q in hand, the remark in the quantum universe definition — that a ground ring limits which block decompositions it can carry — becomes concrete. The invertibility clauses of axiom 4 are quantified over the universe's own blocks, so they constrain the pair (R, \mathbf{C}) and not R alone.

That limit is real. In \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}] the units are exactly \pm q^{k}, while each quantum integer is a monomial times a product of cyclotomic polynomials \Phi_d of positive degree — [2]_q = q^{-1}\Phi_4(q), [3]_q = q^{-2}\Phi_3\Phi_6, [4]_q = q^{-3}\Phi_4\Phi_8. No [m]_q with m \geq 2 is a unit there, so over that ring the block index collapses to the trivial block: the axioms are satisfiable, but only degenerately, and none of the Hecke decompositions of the later chapters fit. Inverting the cyclotomics is what makes a non-degenerate universe available:

  R \;=\; \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]\bigl[\, \Phi_d(q)^{-1} \;:\; d \geq 2 \,\bigr],

whose spectrum is the q-line with the roots of unity of order \geq 2 removed. Starting at d = 1 would additionally delete q = 1, which the classical limit needs, and nothing requires it: q^{n} - 1 = (q-1)\,[n]_q, so q^n - 1 is a unit exactly when q - 1 is, and the constructs inverting q - 1 live past the archimedean wall.

This is a choice of instance, not a strengthening of the definition. Call a pair (R, q) q-generic when q and every \Phi_d(q), d \geq 2, are invertible in R. The property belongs to the construction of a Hecke-type universe, where it is what makes the axiom-4 invertibility conditions hold. It is deliberately not a hypothesis of the quantum-universe definition, which asks only for a commutative ring. The ring above is the initial q-generic ring, so any other base with the property — \mathbb{Q}(q), a real algebra at the aether anchor, a neighbouring convention's Laurent ring — receives a unique map from it and inherits the construction. The map runs outward; no universe is asked to embed in this ring, and injectivity is never required — the evaluation at q = 1 is not injective, and must not be.
thm:aether-parameter-exists: Theorem Existence of the aether parameter. For any quantum observable universe, the parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) exists and is distinct from roots of unity. In the archimedean realization, it specializes to a real-valued field q(p) \ge 1 interpolating the differential.
